Framework seven, Placebo Tests. These are the natural companion to DiD and other quasi experimental methods. The logic is straightforward. Run your analysis on a period, group, or outcome where the treatment could not possibly have had an effect. If you still see an effect, your method has a problem. In our ad example, you would run your DiD analysis but pretend the ad launched one month earlier than it actually did. If you see a six point effect in this fake pre period, your parallel trends assumption is violated, and you should not trust the real estimate either. Passing a placebo test does not prove your estimate is right. But failing one is a strong signal that something is wrong. Think of it as a necessary condition, not a sufficient one.

Framework eight is Manski Bounds. This is for when you want to be brutally honest about what the data can and cannot tell you. Instead of making strong assumptions to get a precise point estimate, Manski bounds give you a range, the worst case and best case treatment effects compatible with observed data under minimal assumptions. In our example, suppose twenty percent of agents have missing voting intention data. Without assuming anything about why data is missing, the ATE could be anywhere from negative twelve to positive twenty eight percentage points. That is a wide interval, but it is honest. Now, if you are willing to add a mild assumption, say that ad exposure never decreases voting intention, the bounds tighten to positive two to positive fourteen. Still wide, but at least the entire interval is positive, suggesting the ad likely helps. The power of Manski bounds is intellectual honesty. The cost is precision.
